content.title: ‘One Battle After Another’ Is Paul Thomas Anderson's Most Personal Film
content.text: This story contains spoilers for One Battle After Another.By now it’s well-documented that Paul Thomas Anderson's Phantom Thread was partly inspired by Anderson’s relationship with his longtime partner Maya Rudolph. “I was very sick with the flu and my wife looked at me with tenderness that made me think, ‘I wonder if she wants to keep me this way, maybe for a week or two,’” he told Collider in 2018, while explaining what had sparked the idea for the story. The sheer rarity of Anderson sharing such details about his private life has contributed to Phantom Thread’s unofficial reputation as the director’s most personal film—but that may be about to change. Bob Ferguson, the protagonist of Anderson’s 10th feature One Battle After Another, which opens this week, reads as an even-closer analog for PTA than the persnickety Reynolds Woodcock did, and although Anderson has not explicitly spoken of any connections between himself and Leonardo DiCaprio’s One Battle character, the film contends with modern themes in a way that mirrors his own artistic journey, making the film feel like his most reflexive work yet.Loosely inspired by Thomas Pynchon’s 1990 novel Vineland, One Battle follows Bob, a middle-aged ex-revolutionary who has been living off the grid raising his daughter Willa (Chase Infiniti) after the disappearance of her mother (Teyana Taylor) 16 years prior. As Willa comes of age, life in her father’s bubble begins to feel constricting, and she craves a more conventional teenage life—one where she’s allowed to have a smartphone, one where her dad doesn’t make her memorize cryptic code phrases to suss out narcs. Bob struggles to curb his protective paternal instincts, which would be fairly typical for any father of a teenage girl, if only they weren’t exacerbated by the paranoia that has come from living on the run; though Bob made it out of the renegade life safely, many of his comrades wound up locked up, missing, or dead. “I wanted to protect you,” Bob explains to Willa. When his worst fears come true and Willa goes missing, Bob is forced to reanimate his past self and also dive headfirst into the modern world from which he has so carefully distanced himself for 16 years.It's been 23 years since Anderson has directed a film set in the present. Every film he’s made since 2002’s Punch-Drunk Love has been a a 20th-century period piece: There Will Be Blood (set mostly in the early 1900s), The Master and Phantom Thread (set in the 1950s), Inherent Vice and Licorice Pizza (set in the ‘70s, forming a three-peat with 1997’s Boogie Nights). In this regard, he’s been in good company; from Quentin Tarantino to Martin Scorsese to Steven Spielberg, none of America’s most canonized living auteurs have made a movie with a contemporary setting since roughly 2007, when the first iPhone was launched. There’s many theories about why this is, particularly if you’re unfortunate enough to be on Film Twitter. These old guys overly romanticize the past. They fear or otherwise resent the younger generations. They think smartphones can’t be cinematic. And so on.I subscribe to none of these theories (and frankly don’t care if Scorsese never makes a movie with iPhones in it—that’s what we have Park Chan-wook for.) I admit I felt a glimmer of panic when I saw a One Battle trailer that featured a joke about Bob not understanding a non-binary person’s pronouns—Oh God, I thought, is PTA making a modern movie to dunk on wokeness? My GOAT might be washed—but after seeing the scene in context, I was relieved to be wrong. Many of the film’s comedic beats come from Bob’s difficulty adapting to the times—seemingly ironic given his leftist leanings, but actually perfectly logical for 1) a Gen Xer who doesn’t use the Internet and 2) a former guerrilla for whom activism meant armed resistance, not posting infographics—but he’s the butt of the joke more often than he’s not. When Bob berates a younger comrade over the phone who refuses to share privileged information with Bob unless he recites the proper password, we are meant to laugh at the bureaucratic absurdity (heightened for satirical effect, as when he accuses Bob of “invading his space” verbally), but we are also meant to laugh at Bob’s sheer ineptitude. This fucking guy has been getting stoned in the woods for 16 years and doesn’t know how anything works anymore.When we meet Sergio (Benicio Del Toro), Bob’s confidant and Willa’s martial arts instructor, we see a revolutionary who has, by contrast, gracefully evolved. Sergio runs a safe house for immigrant families needing refuge from ICE, which his cool, calm demeanor makes evident he has been doing for a long time; as he moves steadily through the house making preparations for a raid, he simultaneously advises a hapless, panicking Bob without even breaking his stride.The film pokes fun without punching down, and in many ways it feels like Anderson is making fun of himself. 30 years ago, Anderson was something of a renegade in Hollywood: he decided film school was a sham and dropped out, he battled with studios over the content and runtimes of his early films but was ultimately affirmed by their success, he was welcomed under the wings of his filmmaking idols Robert Altman, Jonathan Demme and Stanley Kubrick, he beefed with Burt Reynolds, and racked up multiple Oscar nominations and a reputation as an iconoclastic artist all by the time he turned 30.Today, Anderson is another 55-year-old San Fernando Valley dad. With Rudolph he shares four children, aged between 12 to 19—three of whom are girls—whom he presumably shuttles to school and occasionally accompanies to Taylor Swift concerts. That's not to say the guy has lost his edge, but rather to contextualize some of the themes we see in One Battle, particularly the high-octane Girl Dad energy permeating throughout. (Even the needle drops are straight from the Sentimental Dad songbook: Steely Dan’s “Dirty Work” and Tom Petty’s “American Girl” both get prominent placements.)Bob’s relationship with Willa also embodies nuances specific to the experience of a white dad raising mixed-race children––another layer that reflects Anderson’s reality (Rudolph’s, too: after her mother, Minnie Riperton, passed away when Maya was six, she was raised by her father Richard Rudolph, who is white.) There’s so much about Willa that Bob, by his own admission, doesn’t understand and that pronounces the absence of her mother—“I don’t know how to do her hair, man,” he laments to Sergio—and the more we learn about the forces behind her mother’s disappearance, the more we understand the danger Willa could be in. Anderson has said he initially began writing One Battle 20 years ago, around the time his first daughter was born. For it to finally come to fruition in the hellscape of 2025 feels like appropriate, even necessary, timing—the film wouldn’t be what it is without having marinated in Anderson’s mind as he watched two tumultuous decades unfold through his and his family’s eyes.Overall, the film’s politics are more gestural than doctrinal—the Dr. Strangelove-coded bits about a clandestine cabal of white supremacists, while funny, are knowingly Not That Deep—but for Anderson to engage at all with the concept of racism or to depict immigration officers being held at gunpoint by left-wing vigilantes is meaningful for how significantly it differs from his otherwise apolitical body of work. (The only other film that might compare, content-wise, is Inherent Vice, which incidentally also derives from Pynchon and similarly follows a maladapted hippie lost in time.) One Battle also features more actors of color than any of Anderson’s previous films. Not to give more credit than he’s due—I still haven’t forgotten about those lame Asian jokes in Licorice Pizza—but it is reassuring to see him branch out.By the end of the film, once Bob and Willa have reunited and she is teaching him how to use his new iPhone, two affirming transformations have taken place. Bob has loosened his grip on their way of life, welcoming a new dynamic with his daughter in which she’s the one teaching him how to connect with the world. And Anderson, as an artist, has cracked the seal on a new era in which he permits a broader vision of the world—its culture, its technology, its conflicts—to inform and enrich his work. Like Bob, Anderson is an aging rebel reckoning with the nature of time, and with the responsibility he bears as a parent. In One Battle, both men make room for growth by opening the door to a modern world they once kept at bay.
